All topics · Statistics · Lesson 12 · C&B §2.1

Functions of a random variable: one idea, two formulas, one transform

Two blocks. A focused reading (about 15 minutes), then the lesson (about 25 minutes, plus about 10 more if you open the "Go deeper" boxes). Two wins: find the pdf of Y = g(X) and prove the formula; prove the probability integral transform and use it to simulate.

How this lesson works

This lesson moves faster than the Chapter 1 lessons. Each part gives the core idea in a short worked example, then asks two or three questions. Under most parts there is a closed box marked Go deeper: the proofs' fine print and the cases where the simple version breaks. Open one whenever a question stumps you (a missed question's hint will point to it), or when you're curious. If everything lands, skip them.

Number and formula boxes take expressions: type * for ×, /, ^ for powers, sqrt( ), exp( ) and log( ) (natural log). When you get one right, say honestly whether you knew it or guessed.

Reading (about 15 minutes)

Casella & Berger, Statistical Inference, §2.1 "Distributions of Functions of a Random Variable", pp. 47–55. Read these parts:

  1. pp. 47–48: from the start of the section through Example 2.1.1 (the binomial). This is the one idea the rest builds on.
  2. pp. 50–51: from "When transformations are made, it is important to keep track of the sample spaces" through Theorem 2.1.5 and its two-line proof.
  3. pp. 52–53: Example 2.1.7 (\(Y = X^2\)) and Theorem 2.1.8. Example 2.1.9 uses the normal distribution, which Chapter 3 covers; read it for the shape of the argument only.
  4. pp. 54–55: Theorem 2.1.10 (the probability integral transformation), its proof, and the last paragraph on generating random samples.

Skip: Example 2.1.2 (\(\sin^2\), pp. 49–50; glance at Figure 2.1.1) and Example 2.1.6 (inverted gamma, pp. 51–52).

Notation traps.

  • \(g^{-1}\) in (2.1.1) is the inverse image: it takes a set and returns the set of \(x\) that land in it. It is a set even when \(g\) has no inverse function. Only when \(g\) is monotone does \(g^{-1}(y)\) mean a single number.
  • \(\mathcal{X}\) and \(\mathcal{Y}\) (curly letters) are the support sets in (2.1.7), where the densities are positive. They are not the random variables \(X\) and \(Y\).
  • (2.1.13) defines \(F_X^{-1}(y) = \inf\{x : F_X(x) \ge y\}\), which still works where the cdf is flat and has no ordinary inverse.

In (2.1.2), \(P(Y \in A) = P(X \in g^{-1}(A))\). Why is \(g^{-1}(A)\) a set of \(x\) values rather than one number? Give a \(g\) and an \(A\) where it contains more than one point.

Reading note. Any g that isn't one-to-one: g(x) = x², A = {4} gives {−2, 2}; or A an interval. The point: several x can map into A.

Theorem 2.1.3(a) (\(g\) increasing) works for any \(X\), but part (b) (\(g\) decreasing) adds "\(X\) is a continuous random variable". Where in the argument before the theorem does continuity get used?

Reading note. For decreasing g, {g(X) ≤ y} = {X ≥ g⁻¹(y)}, and P(X ≥ x) = 1 − F_X(x) only when P(X = x) = 0, which continuity gives. Answer "the second equality / P(X ≥ x) vs P(X > x)" or equivalent is right.

In the proof of Theorem 2.1.10, the last step is \(F_X(F_X^{-1}(y)) = y\), justified by "continuity of \(F_X\)". Why would that step fail if \(X\) were discrete?

Reading note. A discrete cdf jumps, so it skips values: for some y in (0, 1) no x has F_X(x) = y, and F_X(F_X^{-1}(y)) is the top of a jump, bigger than y. (Equivalently, F_X(X) takes only countably many values, so it can't be uniform.)

What surprised or confused you in the reading?

Why this lesson

Chapter 1 gave you a random variable's distribution. Most quantities you care about are functions of one: a log return, a squared error, a waiting time measured in different units, a test statistic. You want their distributions without going back to the sample space every time. One idea does all of it, and the rest of the section is that idea worked out for the common cases:

An event about \(Y = g(X)\) is an event about \(X\). \(Y \in A\) happens exactly when \(X\) lands in the set of \(x\) values that \(g\) sends into \(A\). So \(P(Y \in A) = P(X \in g^{-1}(A))\).

Recap: cdf, pdf and support (Chapter 1). The cdf is \(F_X(x) = P(X \le x)\). A continuous \(X\) has a pdf with \(F_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f_X(t)\,dt\), so \(f_X = F_X'\) wherever \(f_X\) is continuous. The support \(\mathcal{X}\) is where \(f_X > 0\). Outside it, \(f_X = 0\).

Part 1 · Translate the event (about 4 minutes)

From the reading (pp. 47–48).

A discrete case: just sum. \(X\) is binomial(\(n, p\)), the number of successes, and \(Y = n - X\) counts the failures. \(Y = y\) exactly when \(X = n - y\), one point. So \(P(Y = y) = P(X = n - y) = \binom{n}{n-y} p^{n-y}(1-p)^{y}\).

Recognise it. \(\binom{n}{n-y} = \binom{n}{y}\), so this is \(\binom{n}{y}(1-p)^{y}p^{n-y}\): a binomial(\(n, 1-p\)). Failures are "successes" with probability \(1 - p\). (Example 2.1.1.)

When several \(x\) map to one \(y\), add them. For a discrete \(X\), \(P(Y = y) = \sum_{x \in g^{-1}(y)} P(X = x)\): every \(x\) that \(g\) sends to \(y\) contributes.

\(X\) takes each of the values \(-2, -1, 0, 1, 2\) with probability \(\tfrac15\), and \(Y = X^2\). What is \(P(Y = 1)\)? Answer as a decimal or a fraction (0.10 means 10%).

\(Y = 1\) when \(X = -1\) or \(X = 1\): the inverse image of \(\{1\}\) is \(\{-1, 1\}\). So \(P(Y = 1) = \tfrac15 + \tfrac15 = \tfrac25\).

Part 2 · Monotone g: the cdf method, then the formula (about 8 minutes)

From the reading (pp. 50–52).

Start from the cdf, the one thing defined for every random variable. \(X\) is uniform on \((0, 1)\), so \(F_X(x) = x\) there. Let \(Y = -\log X\). Since \(X\) is in \((0, 1)\), \(Y\) is in \((0, \infty)\). For \(y > 0\), translate the event: \(-\log X \le y\) means \(\log X \ge -y\), which means \(X \ge e^{-y}\). Try the next line before revealing it: what is \(F_Y(y)\)?

\(F_Y(y) = P(X \ge e^{-y}) = 1 - F_X(e^{-y}) = 1 - e^{-y}\). The inequality flipped because \(-\log\) is decreasing. (The step from \(P(X \ge \cdot)\) to \(1 - F_X(\cdot)\) uses \(P(X = e^{-y}) = 0\): \(X\) is continuous.)

Differentiate to get the pdf. \(f_Y(y) = e^{-y}\) for \(y > 0\): the exponential distribution. This is Example 2.1.4.

Now in general. Write \(g^{-1}\) for the inverse function. If \(g\) is increasing, \(F_Y(y) = F_X(g^{-1}(y))\); the chain rule gives \(f_Y(y) = f_X(g^{-1}(y))\,\tfrac{d}{dy}g^{-1}(y)\). If \(g\) is decreasing, \(F_Y(y) = 1 - F_X(g^{-1}(y))\), so \(f_Y(y) = -f_X(g^{-1}(y))\,\tfrac{d}{dy}g^{-1}(y)\), which is positive because \(g^{-1}\) is decreasing too.

One formula for both (Theorem 2.1.5). For \(y\) in the support \(\mathcal{Y}\),

$$ f_Y(y) = f_X\big(g^{-1}(y)\big)\,\left\lvert \frac{d}{dy}\,g^{-1}(y) \right\rvert , $$

and \(f_Y(y) = 0\) outside \(\mathcal{Y}\). The absolute value covers the sign in the decreasing case. The theorem assumes \(f_X\) is continuous on \(\mathcal{X}\) and \(g^{-1}\) has a continuous derivative on \(\mathcal{Y}\): those are exactly what the chain-rule step needs to turn the cdf into a pdf.

Say it this way: "The pdf of \(Y\) is the pdf of \(X\) at the matching point, times how much \(g^{-1}\) stretches or squeezes lengths there." Not this: "\(f_Y(y) = f_X(g^{-1}(y))\)." Densities are probability per unit length, so changing the units changes the density. That's what the derivative factor measures.

Casella & Berger, Exercise 2.1(b). \(X\) has pdf \(f_X(x) = 7e^{-7x}\) for \(x > 0\), and \(Y = 4X + 3\). What is the pdf of \(Y\) at \(y = 5\)? (An expression, e.g. with exp( ), or a decimal to 4 places.)

\(g^{-1}(y) = (y - 3)/4\), with derivative \(\tfrac14\). So \(f_Y(y) = \tfrac74 e^{-7(y-3)/4}\) for \(y > 3\) (the support moved from \((0, \infty)\) to \((3, \infty)\)). At \(y = 5\): \(\tfrac74 e^{-7/2}\).

Casella & Berger, Exercise 2.1(a). \(X\) has pdf \(f_X(x) = 42x^5(1 - x)\) for \(0 < x < 1\), and \(Y = X^3\). What is \(f_Y\!\left(\tfrac18\right)\)? (A fraction or decimal is fine.)

\(g^{-1}(y) = y^{1/3}\) and \(\tfrac{d}{dy} y^{1/3} = \tfrac13 y^{-2/3}\). So \(f_Y(y) = 42\,y^{5/3}(1 - y^{1/3}) \cdot \tfrac13 y^{-2/3} = 14\,y\,(1 - y^{1/3})\) on \((0, 1)\). At \(y = \tfrac18\): \(14 \cdot \tfrac18 \cdot \tfrac12 = \tfrac78\).

Prove that if \(X\) is continuous with pdf \(f_X\) and \(g\) is decreasing with a differentiable inverse, then \(f_Y(y) = -f_X(g^{-1}(y))\,\tfrac{d}{dy}g^{-1}(y)\) for \(y\) in the support of \(Y = g(X)\). Justify each step (3–6 lines of plain text).

F_Y(y) = P(g(X) ≤ y) = P(X ≥ g^{-1}(y)) (g decreasing reverses the inequality) = 1 − F_X(g^{-1}(y)) (X continuous, so the point has probability 0); differentiate with the chain rule: f_Y(y) = −f_X(g^{-1}(y)) (g^{-1})'(y). Got it: the flipped inequality justified by "decreasing", and the chain rule. Can't tell: missing why P(X ≥ x) = 1 − F_X(x). Not yet: keeps ≤ (no flip).

Go deeper: where the formula comes from, and why part (b) needs a continuous X

Beyond the reading, except the remark on continuity, which the book makes before Theorem 2.1.3.

The derivative factor, with numbers. If \(X\) is uniform on \((0, 1)\) (density 1) and \(Y = 4X\), then \(Y\) is uniform on \((0, 4)\), so its density must be \(\tfrac14\): the same total probability spread over four times the length. The formula agrees: \(g^{-1}(y) = y/4\), with derivative \(\tfrac14\). For a nonlinear \(g\) the stretch varies from point to point, which is why the factor is a derivative evaluated at \(y\).

Why Theorem 2.1.3(b) assumes \(X\) is continuous. For a decreasing \(g\), \(\{g(X) \le y\} = \{X \ge g^{-1}(y)\}\). The step \(P(X \ge x) = 1 - F_X(x)\) is only true when \(P(X = x) = 0\). For a discrete \(X\) the point \(x\) itself can carry probability, and then the formula undercounts. Part (a) never needs that step, so it holds for every \(X\). Try it:

\(X\) is 0 or 1, each with probability \(\tfrac12\), and \(Y = -X\) (a decreasing function of \(X\)). Compute \(F_Y(-1) = P(Y \le -1)\) directly. (Then compare it with what the decreasing-case formula \(1 - F_X(g^{-1}(-1)) = 1 - F_X(1)\) would give.)

\(Y \le -1\) means \(-X \le -1\), so \(X \ge 1\), so \(X = 1\): probability \(\tfrac12\). The formula gives \(1 - F_X(1) = 1 - 1 = 0\), wrong by exactly \(P(X = 1)\), the probability sitting on the boundary point. Continuity makes that boundary probability 0.

Part 3 · Not monotone: split into monotone pieces (about 6 minutes)

From the reading (pp. 52–53).

Same idea, two pieces. Let \(Y = X^2\) for a continuous \(X\). For \(y > 0\), \(X^2 \le y\) means \(-\sqrt y \le X \le \sqrt y\). So \(F_Y(y) = F_X(\sqrt y) - F_X(-\sqrt y)\). (The endpoint \(-\sqrt y\) carries no probability, since \(X\) is continuous.)

Differentiate. By the chain rule, \(f_Y(y) = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt y}\Big(f_X(\sqrt y) + f_X(-\sqrt y)\Big)\). This is (2.1.11). Each term is the monotone formula on one piece: \(x > 0\), where \(g^{-1}(y) = \sqrt y\), and \(x < 0\), where it's \(-\sqrt y\). Both derivatives have absolute value \(\tfrac{1}{2\sqrt y}\).

In general (Theorem 2.1.8): split the support of \(X\) into pieces on which \(g\) is monotone and that each map onto all of \(\mathcal{Y}\), apply the monotone formula on each piece, and add. Points of probability 0 (here \(x = 0\)) can be set aside.

\(X\) has pdf \(f_X(x) = \tfrac32 x^2\) for \(-1 < x < 1\) (0 elsewhere), and \(Y = X^2\). What is \(f_Y\!\left(\tfrac14\right)\)? (A fraction or decimal is fine.)

\(f_Y(y) = \frac{1}{2\sqrt y}\big(\tfrac32 y + \tfrac32 y\big) = \tfrac32\sqrt y\) on \((0, 1)\). At \(y = \tfrac14\): \(\tfrac32 \cdot \tfrac12 = \tfrac34\).

\(X\) is uniform on \((0, 1)\), and a student finds the pdf of \(Y = X^2\) on \((0, 1)\). Which is the first wrong step?

  1. \(f_X(x) = 1\) for \(0 < x < 1\), and \(f_X(x) = 0\) elsewhere.
  2. For \(0 < y < 1\), \(f_Y(y) = \frac{1}{2\sqrt y}\big(f_X(\sqrt y) + f_X(-\sqrt y)\big)\), formula (2.1.11) for a continuous \(X\).
  3. Both \(f_X(\sqrt y)\) and \(f_X(-\sqrt y)\) equal 1, the value of the uniform density.
  4. So \(f_Y(y) = \frac{1}{\sqrt y}\) for \(0 < y < 1\).

\(-\sqrt y\) is negative, outside the support \((0, 1)\), so \(f_X(-\sqrt y) = 0\) and \(f_Y(y) = \frac{1}{2\sqrt y}\). On \((0, 1)\), \(x^2\) is increasing, so there was only one piece all along. The student's \(\frac{1}{\sqrt y}\) integrates to 2 over \((0, 1)\), so it can't be a pdf. That's why the book insists on tracking the support sets.

Go deeper: when the pieces don't line up (Exercise 2.7)

Beyond the reading (the book leaves it to Exercise 2.7).

Theorem 2.1.8 asks every piece to map onto the same set \(\mathcal{Y}\). Sometimes they don't. If \(X\) is uniform on \((-1, 2)\) and \(Y = X^2\): for \(0 < y < 1\), both \(\sqrt y\) and \(-\sqrt y\) are in the support, so two terms. For \(1 < y < 4\), only \(\sqrt y\) is (\(-\sqrt y < -1\)), so one term. The fix is the same idea applied separately on each range of \(y\): sum over the \(x\) in the support that map to that \(y\).

\(X\) is uniform on \((-1, 2)\) (density \(\tfrac13\) there) and \(Y = X^2\). What is \(f_Y(2)\)? (An expression, e.g. with sqrt( ), or a decimal to 4 places.)

For \(y = 2\), only \(x = \sqrt2\) is in \((-1, 2)\). So \(f_Y(2) = \tfrac13 \cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt2} = \frac{1}{6\sqrt2}\). (For \(0 < y < 1\) it would be \(\tfrac23 \cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt y}\); the two ranges together integrate to 1.)

Part 4 · The probability integral transform, and simulation (about 7 minutes)

From the reading (pp. 54–55).

A computer only makes uniform(0, 1) random numbers. How do you turn them into draws from an exponential, or from any distribution you can write a cdf for? Run the question backwards first: what happens when a random variable goes into its own cdf?

Feed a random variable into its own cdf. \(X\) is exponential: \(F_X(x) = 1 - e^{-x}\) for \(x > 0\). Let \(Y = F_X(X)\), a number in \((0, 1)\). For \(0 < y < 1\), translate the event: \(1 - e^{-X} \le y\) means \(X \le -\log(1 - y)\). Predict \(P(Y \le y)\) before revealing.

\(P(Y \le y) = F_X(-\log(1 - y)) = 1 - e^{\log(1 - y)} = y\). That's the cdf of the uniform on \((0, 1)\). The same happens for any rate, and (next step) for any continuous \(X\).

In general (Theorem 2.1.10): for any \(X\) with a continuous cdf, \(F_X(X)\) is uniform on \((0, 1)\). When \(F_X\) is strictly increasing the proof is the same chain: \(P(F_X(X) \le y) = P(X \le F_X^{-1}(y)) = F_X(F_X^{-1}(y)) = y\).

Run it backwards to simulate. If \(U\) is uniform on \((0, 1)\), then \(X = F^{-1}(U)\) has cdf \(F\): \(P(F^{-1}(U) \le x) = P(U \le F(x)) = F(x)\). A computer makes uniform numbers, and inverting the cdf turns them into any distribution you can write a cdf for.

Say it this way: "Plugging a continuous random variable into its own cdf gives a uniform(0, 1); plugging a uniform into an inverse cdf gives that distribution." Not this: "\(F_X(X)\) has the same distribution as \(X\)."

You want to simulate \(X\) with cdf \(F(x) = 1 - e^{-2x}\) for \(x > 0\). The computer gives the uniform number \(u = 0.5\). Using \(x = F^{-1}(u)\), what \(x\) do you report? (An expression, e.g. with log( ), the natural log, or a decimal to 3 places.)

\(1 - e^{-2x} = u\) gives \(x = -\tfrac12\log(1 - u)\). With \(u = 0.5\): \(x = \tfrac12\log 2 \approx 0.347\), the median of this distribution, as it should be, since half the uniforms fall below 0.5.

Your proof (3–6 lines of plain text is fine). \(X\) has a continuous cdf \(F_X\) that is strictly increasing, and \(Y = F_X(X)\). Prove that \(P(Y \le y) = y\) for \(0 < y < 1\), so \(Y\) is uniform on \((0, 1)\). Justify each step.

For 0 < y < 1: P(Y ≤ y) = P(F_X(X) ≤ y) = P(X ≤ F_X^{-1}(y)) (F_X strictly increasing, so it has an inverse and applying it keeps the inequality) = F_X(F_X^{-1}(y)) (definition of the cdf) = y (F_X continuous, so it takes every value in (0, 1) and F_X^{-1}(y) exists). Got it: the chain with the inversion step justified by "strictly increasing". Can't tell: the chain right but no justification for inverting. Not yet: a false step (e.g. treating F_X(X) as having the distribution of X).

\(P(Y \le y) = P(F_X(X) \le y) = P(X \le F_X^{-1}(y)) = F_X(F_X^{-1}(y)) = y\). Inverting is allowed because \(F_X\) is strictly increasing; continuity makes \(F_X^{-1}(y)\) exist for every \(y\) in \((0, 1)\).

Go deeper: flat cdfs, and why a discrete X fails

Flat stretches: from the reading, pp. 54–55. The discrete case: beyond the reading.

Flat stretches. If \(F_X\) is constant on an interval \([x_1, x_2]\), that interval carries probability 0, and \(F_X\) has no ordinary inverse there. The book's (2.1.13) uses \(F_X^{-1}(y) = \inf\{x : F_X(x) \ge y\}\), the left end of the flat stretch. The step \(P(F_X(X) \le y) = P(X \le F_X^{-1}(y))\) still holds as an equality of probabilities, because \(X\) almost never lands in the flat stretch (pp. 54–55).

Discrete \(X\): no. A discrete cdf jumps, so \(F_X(X)\) takes only a few values. Try it:

\(X\) is 0 or 1, each with probability \(\tfrac12\), so \(F_X(0) = \tfrac12\) and \(F_X(1) = 1\). Let \(Y = F_X(X)\). What is \(P(Y \le 0.7)\)? (A uniform(0, 1) would give 0.7.)

\(Y\) is \(\tfrac12\) (when \(X = 0\)) or 1 (when \(X = 1\)). \(Y \le 0.7\) only when \(Y = \tfrac12\): probability \(\tfrac12\), not 0.7. The transform needs a continuous cdf; Exercise 2.10 shows what survives for discrete \(X\).

Wrap-up

  • One idea: \(P(Y \in A) = P(X \in g^{-1}(A))\). Discrete: sum over the inverse image. Continuous: translate the cdf's event.
  • Monotone \(g\): \(f_Y(y) = f_X(g^{-1}(y))\,\lvert \tfrac{d}{dy}g^{-1}(y)\rvert\) on the support of \(Y\). Track the support.
  • Not monotone: split into monotone pieces and add.
  • Probability integral transform: \(F_X(X)\) is uniform(0, 1) for a continuous cdf; \(F^{-1}(U)\) simulates \(F\).

Extra practice (optional)

Problems from Casella & Berger, Chapter 2 exercises (pp. 76–77), easiest first. Answers are in the Casella & Berger solutions manual.

  1. Exercise 2.1(c): \(Y = X^2\) with \(f_X(x) = 30x^2(1-x)^2\) on \((0, 1)\). Check that your pdf integrates to 1.
  2. Exercise 2.2(a): \(Y = X^2\) with \(X\) uniform on \((0, 1)\).
  3. Exercise 2.3: a discrete transformation (geometric \(X\), \(Y = X/(X+1)\)): give the pmf of \(Y\).
  4. Exercise 2.7: the uneven-pieces situation from the second Go deeper box, with a non-uniform density.
  5. Exercise 2.10: what the probability integral transform says when \(X\) is discrete.

Extra reading: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability, 2nd ed., §8.1 "Change of variables" (from p. 368) for the same formula with more worked examples, and §5.3 "Universality of the Uniform" (from p. 224), their name for the probability integral transform.

Extra article: Luc Devroye, Non-Uniform Random Variate Generation (1986), Chapter 2, §2 "The inversion method" (chapter PDF, free from the author). It's the standard reference on turning uniform random numbers into other distributions, and its first method is the one in Part 4, with what to do when \(F^{-1}\) has no closed form.
